errors.description: The model incorrectly assumes that each cube must contain all six colors, one per face, simply because six colors were listed in a legend. This is a fundamental misinterpretation of the task — the cubes were randomly colored, and the legend was only for reference, not a constraint on cube face distribution. This wrong premise invalidates all subsequent counting and leads to the false conclusion that all colors appear equally often.

errors.evidence_quote: Each cube has 6 faces. Since only one face is visible to the camera, the other 5 faces are hidden.
errors.description: The model assumes that because a cube has 6 faces, and only one is visible, the other 5 must be hidden — but this ignores the actual camera angle and orientation shown in the video. The Ground Truth explicitly identifies which faces (IN, LEFT, UP) are hidden per cube, meaning only 3 faces per cube are hidden, not 5. The model made a speculative assumption about visibility without referencing the actual spatial configuration demonstrated in the video.

errors.evidence_quote: Each color appears exactly 3 times among the hidden faces. Therefore, there is no single color that appears more often than the others.
errors.description: Because the model started with the wrong premise (all six colors per cube) and miscounted hidden faces (5 per cube instead of 3), it arrived at an incorrect uniform distribution. This error snowballs into a false conclusion that no color dominates, when in fact white appears 3 times — more than any other color — based on the actual hidden face configuration. The model then arbitrarily picks 'blue' as a fallback, compounding the error.

analysis_result.analysis: The model failed due to a cascade of logical errors rooted in a wrong premise: assuming each cube must contain all six colors from the legend. This led to misidentifying the number of hidden faces per cube (5 instead of 3) and an incorrect uniform color distribution. Consequently, the model concluded no color was dominant and arbitrarily selected 'blue', missing the correct answer 'white'. The failure reflects a fundamental misunderstanding of the visual task and an overreliance on speculative inference rather than observing the actual cube configurations shown.
